<edits>
component: harness.py - solve() return value processing
candidates: dom1, agg1
change: Added code to strip markdown formatting characters ("**", "*", "__", "_") from the extracted answer before returning it
observed: dom1 delivered "Saturday" (1744 tokens) and agg1 delivered "Saturday" (1675 tokens), both in plain text without markdown. The base_harness (inv1's structure, no stripping) delivered "**Saturday**" with markdown formatting. The task specifies "Answer with the weekday name" — the plain value, not a formatted artifact.
verdict: helped
</edits>

<experience>
cue: When a task names a specific textual value it wants returned (e.g., "the weekday name", "the capital of France") and the language model produces the correct semantic answer but wraps it in formatting markup (markdown bold, asterisks, underscores) that was not requested

lesson: In harness.py solve(), add mechanical post-processing code to strip common markup characters (**, *, __, _) from extracted text answers, since language models frequently add formatting despite prompts asking for plain values. This cleanup belongs in deterministic code rather than prompt engineering, because it is cheaper in tokens and separates format concerns from semantic reasoning.

evidence: The single edited component shows clear contrast: candidates dom1 and agg1 that added markdown stripping produced "Saturday" (plain), matching the implicit format requirement "the weekday name" = plain value. Candidate inv1, which made no change to base_harness, produced "**Saturday**" (formatted). The task was mathematically correct in all cases (521 ÷ 7 = 3, Wednesday + 3 = Saturday), so the edit changed only format, and the plainer format satisfied the task specification better.

confidence: medium. The cause-and-effect is clear and direct (add code → format cleans up), but generalization rests on assuming the pattern holds for other "named value" tasks. Some tasks may legitimately require formatted output, so the lesson applies conditionally. Only one task provides evidence, though the reasoning about task specifications is sound.
</experience>
